findings.bug: For a string schema whose example is a single double-quote character (\"), the code enters the unwrap branch and calls example.substring(1, example.length()-1) = substring(1,0), which throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException.
findings.why_real: startsWith(\"\") and endsWith(\"\") are both true for a length-1 string equal to '\"' (the same char is first and last), so the branch runs even though there is nothing between the quotes; substring(1,0) has begin>end. Verified with the JDK: `\"\"`.substring(1,0) throws java.lang.StringIndexOutOfBoundsException Range [1, 0). A string example of a single quote is valid OpenAPI input.
findings.how_to_prove: Build a Schema with type=string and example="\"" (one double-quote char) and call fixStringModel; expected: example becomes empty string; actual: StringIndexOutOfBoundsException thrown.

findings.bug: Uses reference inequality m.getExample() != "" instead of !"".equals(m.getExample()); the != on String is an identity check that is essentially always true, so the intended 'skip empty-string example' guard never fires.
findings.why_real: JLS: != on reference types compares object identity, not value; an example value equal to "" but not interned to the same reference passes the guard. Sibling code elsewhere uses .equals for string comparison. The intended semantics (non-empty example) are not enforced.
findings.how_to_prove: Pass a Schema whose example is a fresh empty String (new String("")); schemaContainsExample returns true though the example is empty, whereas the intended guard should return false.

findings.bug: Reads the 'x-original-swagger-version' extension using containsValue(key) instead of containsKey(key); the branch tests whether some extension VALUE equals the literal string 'x-original-swagger-version', which is never the case, so the original-version lookup is dead and it always falls back to openAPI.getOpenapi().
findings.why_real: The value is stored under the key 'x-original-swagger-version' (then read via get(xOriginalSwaggerVersion) as a key on the next line), so the guard must be containsKey. containsValue tests the wrong side of the map. The get() on the following line confirms key-based access was intended.
findings.how_to_prove: Create an OpenAPI whose openapi field is '3.0.1' but with extension {x-original-swagger-version: '3.1.0'}; expected (containsKey intent): method reads '3.1.0' and returns true; actual: containsValue is false, falls back to '3.0.1', returns false.

findings.bug: A page token of just "-" (or "--") reaches the range branch, where part.split("-") returns a length-0 array, so rangeParts[0] throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of being handled.
findings.why_real: Verified in a JVM: "-".split("-") has length 0 (trailing empty strings are stripped by String.split with the default limit). The catch clause on line 822 only catches NumberFormatException, so the AIOOBE from rangeParts[0] escapes. The public entry parsePageList(String) (line 636) only catches NumberFormatException too, so it also propagates to the caller, breaking the class's own contract of gracefully returning List.of(1) for bad input.
findings.how_to_prove: GeneralUtils.parsePageList("-", 10, false) -> expected List.of(1) (per the NumberFormatException fallback contract) or a valid page list; actual throws java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Directly: handlePart("-", 10, 0) throws AIOOBE.

findings.bug: Any page token containing 'n' that is not a valid n-expression (e.g. "nx", "n)") makes handlePart call evaluateNFunc, which throws IllegalArgumentException on a failed format check; handlePart does not catch it, so it escapes uncaught.
findings.why_real: evaluateNFunc (lines 700-705) throws IllegalArgumentException when the expression fails the math-expression regex; handlePart's n-branch (lines 801-807) invokes it with no try/catch, and the outer parsePageList(String) (line 642) catches only NumberFormatException, so an invalid page string produces an uncaught IllegalArgumentException instead of the intended List.of(1) fallback. The same escape occurs when totalPages > 10000, because evaluateNFunc rejects maxValue > 10000 (line 692).
findings.how_to_prove: GeneralUtils.parsePageList("nx", 10, false) -> expected graceful fallback List.of(1); actual throws java.lang.IllegalArgumentException("Invalid expression format: nx").

findings.bug: getInstance(processType, liveUpdates) memoizes the executor via computeIfAbsent keyed only on processType, so the liveUpdates flag is captured only on the first call; later calls with a different liveUpdates value silently reuse the original setting.
findings.why_real: computeIfAbsent(processType, ...) (line 52) only runs the mapping function on first insertion, and liveUpdates is read inside that lambda. A second call getInstance(TESSERACT, false) after getInstance(TESSERACT, true) returns the cached instance with liveUpdates=true, contradicting the caller's requested value.
findings.how_to_prove: Call getInstance(Processes.TESSERACT, true) then getInstance(Processes.TESSERACT, false); expected an executor honoring liveUpdates=false, actual returns the same instance with liveUpdates=true (observable via a getter or by verifying identical object reference while the flag differs).

findings.bug: limitAppEquals treats "" as equal to "default", and "default" as equal to null, but "" is NOT equal to null, violating the transitivity requirement of Object.equals.
findings.why_real: The Object.equals contract (JLS / java.lang.Object Javadoc) requires transitivity: if a.equals(b) and b.equals(c) then a.equals(c). Here with a="", b="default", c=null: equals("","default") returns "default".equals("default")=true; equals("default",null) returns (str2==null)=true; but equals("",null) returns "default".equals(null)=false. hashCode() (line 133) collapses all three into the same bucket, so this is used as a HashSet key in RuleManager/DegradeRuleManager where the contract matters.
findings.how_to_prove: Build three AbstractRule instances r1,r2,r3 with same resource and limitApp of "", "default", null respectively. Assert r1.equals(r2) && r2.equals(r3) but !r1.equals(r3) -> the last assertion currently passes (r1 != r3) proving transitivity is broken; equals contract requires all three to agree.

findings.bug: The guard uses OR (keyCertChainFilePath != null || keyFilePath != null) but the body immediately dereferences getKeyFilePath().endsWith(".jks"), throwing NullPointerException when only keyCertChainFilePath is configured and keyFilePath is null.
findings.why_real: If keyCertChainFilePath is non-null and keyFilePath is null, the OR condition is true so the block is entered, and line 126 calls .endsWith on a null keyFilePath. The sibling null-safe handling of keyFilePassword (line 129/135) shows the author knew these fields may be null; the OR guard should be AND (both required) to match the two-File keyManager/keyStore calls that need both paths.
findings.how_to_prove: Construct a RedisConnectionConfig with sslEnable=true, keyCertChainFilePath set to a path, keyFilePath=null, and call initSslOptions -> expected: no NPE (skip key material) or a validated error; actual: NullPointerException at getKeyFilePath().endsWith(".jks").

findings.bug: When a value is absent, putIfAbsent inserts a fresh AtomicInteger(0) and returns null, so the decrement branch is skipped, leaving a spurious 0-valued entry that is never removed, permanently polluting the thread-count cache.
findings.why_real: The intended behavior (mirror of addThreadCount) is to decrement an existing counter and remove it when it reaches <=0. For an absent value, putIfAbsent stores a 0 entry then the code does nothing because oldValue==null, so the just-created 0 entry is orphaned and never removed by the <=0 cleanup, unlike the value it was decrementing. This is an unbounded resource/map leak keyed by arbitrary request parameter values.
findings.how_to_prove: Call decreaseThreadCount(arg) for an arg that was never added (threadCountMap for index 0 initialized). Then inspect getThreadCountMap().get(0).get(arg): expected null (no entry created), actual an AtomicInteger with value 0 remains in the cache.

findings.bug: GroupMatcher.And.add() throws UnsupportedOperationException because the backing collection is created with Arrays.asList(matchers), which is fixed-size.
findings.why_real: The GroupMatcher interface explicitly declares add(Matcher) with Javadoc '追加匹配器' (append a matcher), but Arrays.asList returns a fixed-size java.util.Arrays$ArrayList whose add() is documented to throw UnsupportedOperationException. The sibling Or() no-arg constructor correctly uses new ArrayList, proving the intended contract.
findings.how_to_prove: new GroupMatcher.And<String>(m1).add(m2) -> expected: matcher appended; actual: throws UnsupportedOperationException.

findings.bug: When an Or group is built via the varargs constructor Or(Matcher...), its add() throws UnsupportedOperationException because that constructor stores Arrays.asList(matchers) (fixed-size).
findings.why_real: Same authority as And: the interface's add() must append, but Or(Matcher...) assigns matchers = Arrays.asList(matchers), which is fixed-size; the no-arg Or() constructor uses a mutable ArrayList, showing the varargs path violates the add() contract.
findings.how_to_prove: new GroupMatcher.Or<String>(m1).add(m2) -> expected: matcher appended; actual: throws UnsupportedOperationException (whereas new Or<>() then add() works).

findings.bug: findProxyRequestPromise(requestId) can return null (the promise is auto-removed after a 60s timeout in TunnelServer.addProxyRequestPromise), yet the code dereferences it with promise.setSuccess(...)/promise.setFailure(...) without a null check, causing a NullPointerException.
findings.why_real: TunnelServer.addProxyRequestPromise schedules removeProxyRequestPromise(requestId) after 60s, so findProxyRequestPromise can legitimately return null for a late/duplicate agent response; unlike requestId (which is null-checked at line 112), the promise itself is never checked before use.
findings.how_to_prove: Send an HTTP_PROXY TextWebSocketFrame whose requestId is not present in proxyRequestPromiseMap (e.g. after expiry) with a valid PROXY_RESPONSE_DATA -> expected: handled/logged; actual: NPE at promise.setSuccess.

findings.bug: oceanbase_oracle is declared with the int expression (1 << 31), which evaluates to Integer.MIN_VALUE (-2147483648) and is sign-extended when widened to the long field 'mask', producing mask=0xFFFFFFFF80000000 instead of the intended single bit; this sets all 33 high bits and collides with polardb, ali_oracle, mock and every subsequent 1L<<n mask.
findings.why_real: Constructor is DbType(long mask); the argument 1 << 31 is int arithmetic (literal 1 is int), so 1<<31 = Integer.MIN_VALUE, and int->long widening sign-extends to 0xFFFFFFFF80000000. Sibling enum constants from index 32 up correctly use the long literal form (1L << 32); oceanbase_oracle should likewise be 1L << 31. The mask field is documented/used as a unique single bit in DbType.of(DbType...) which ORs masks together.
findings.how_to_prove: assertEquals(0x80000000L, DbType.oceanbase_oracle.mask) FAILS: actual is 0xFFFFFFFF80000000L. Also (DbType.oceanbase_oracle.mask & DbType.polardb.mask) expected 0 but is polardb.mask (nonzero); and DbType.of(DbType.oceanbase_oracle) spuriously has the polardb/ali_oracle bits set. Verified by compiling: 1<<31 widened to long yields ffffffff80000000, overlapping 1L<<32 and 1L<<33.

findings.bug: form(String) throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException on a single-quote-character name such as "\"", "'" or "`": the guard startsWith(q) && endsWith(q) is satisfied by a length-1 string equal to the quote char, then substring(1, length()-1) becomes substring(1, 0) which throws.
findings.why_real: For a 1-char string s equal to the quote character, s.startsWith(q) and s.endsWith(q) are both true, and s.length()-1 == 0, so s.substring(1, 0) is called with beginIndex(1) > endIndex(0), which per String.substring's contract throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. This method is reached from WallConfig.isDenyObjects/isDenySchema/isDenyFunction on caller-supplied identifiers.
findings.how_to_prove: WallVisitorUtils.form("\"") -> expected "\"" (or empty string) but actually throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. Same for form("'") and form("`").

findings.bug: removeNameQuotes returns null (instead of the input) for any input of length <= 1, so a legitimate single-character unquoted identifier like "a" is turned into null rather than being returned unchanged.
findings.why_real: The method's contract (per its siblings and name) is to strip surrounding quotes and otherwise return the string; for the non-quoted, non-empty case it returns s unchanged (last line). But the early guard 's.length() <= 1' returns null, conflating a valid 1-char name with the null/empty case, whereas a 1-char name has no surrounding quote pair to strip and should be returned as-is.
findings.how_to_prove: StringUtils.removeNameQuotes("a") -> expected "a" but actual is null; contrast removeNameQuotes("ab") -> "ab" (returned unchanged), showing the length-1 case is inconsistently dropped to null.

findings.bug: getCell(cellnum) checks the upper bound with cellnum>=size but then returns cellList.get(cellnum-1), an off-by-one that throws for cellnum=0 and returns the wrong (previous) cell for any valid index.
findings.why_real: POI's Row.getCell(int) contract returns the cell at the given 0-based column index; here the guard (cellnum>=size) and the access (cellnum-1) are inconsistent. For getCell(0) on a non-empty row it evaluates cellList.get(-1) -> IndexOutOfBoundsException on a perfectly valid argument; for getCell(1) it returns the cell at index 0. Sibling/POI semantics require cellList.get(cellnum).
findings.how_to_prove: CsvRow row = new CsvRow(wb,sheet,0); row.createCell(0); row.createCell(1); row.getCell(0) -> expected the first CsvCell, actual IndexOutOfBoundsException (get(-1)); row.getCell(1) -> expected second cell, actual returns first cell.

findings.bug: getPhysicalNumberOfCells() returns getRowNum() (the row index) instead of the number of cells in the row.
findings.why_real: POI's Row.getPhysicalNumberOfCells() javadoc: 'gets the number of defined cells (NOT number of cells in the actual row!)'. Returning the row index is unrelated to the cell count; correct value is cellList.size().
findings.how_to_prove: CsvRow row = new CsvRow(wb,sheet,5); row.createCell(0); row.createCell(1); row.getPhysicalNumberOfCells() -> expected 2, actual 5 (the rowIndex).

findings.bug: The DataFormatter is cached in a ThreadLocal with no key on (use1904windowing, locale, useScientificFormat); the first call on a thread fixes those settings and every later call on the same thread reuses that formatter, ignoring differing parameters.
findings.why_real: The method takes use1904windowing/locale/useScientificFormat as arguments but only uses them when dataFormatter==null (first call). A second call with different locale/1904 settings on the same thread silently formats with the first call's settings, producing wrong output for valid inputs.
findings.how_to_prove: On one thread call format(date, fmt,..., use1904windowing=false, Locale.US, false) then format(sameData,..., use1904windowing=true, Locale.FRANCE, ...): expected locale/windowing-specific output, actual both formatted with the first (US, 1900) DataFormatter because the cached instance is reused.

findings.bug: Uses BigDecimal.ONE.equals(value) to detect a true value; BigDecimal.equals is scale-sensitive so a numerically-one value with a different scale (e.g. new BigDecimal("1.0")) is treated as false.
findings.why_real: BigDecimal.equals javadoc: two BigDecimals are equal only if equal in value AND scale, so new BigDecimal("1.0").equals(BigDecimal.ONE) is false. The numeric-comparison intent requires compareTo, as the read side (convertToJavaData) returns BigDecimal.ONE/ZERO by value. A value of 1.0 (scale 1) is written as Boolean.FALSE.
findings.how_to_prove: new BigDecimalBooleanConverter().convertToExcelData(new BigDecimal("1.0"), null, null) -> expected WriteCellData(Boolean.TRUE), actual WriteCellData(Boolean.FALSE) because BigDecimal.ONE.equals(new BigDecimal("1.0")) is false.

findings.bug: pagesAvailable = (totalCount / pageSize) + 1 over-reports the page count by one whenever totalCount is an exact multiple of pageSize.
findings.why_real: Correct ceiling division is (totalCount + pageSize - 1) / pageSize. For totalCount=10, pageSize=5 there are exactly 2 pages, but the formula yields 3; the sibling subPageList/calculatePageMetadata never assumes an extra page. The +1 only produces the right answer when totalCount % pageSize != 0.
findings.how_to_prove: PageUtil.subPage(list-of-10, 1, 5).getPagesAvailable() -> expected 2, actual 3.

findings.bug: The byte-stream copy accumulates the copied size in an int (totalBytes) although the method is declared to return long, so counts above 2^31-1 overflow to a negative/wrong value.
findings.why_real: The sibling method copy(Reader,Writer) at line 185 correctly accumulates into a long count. Returning int-widened-to-long means a >2GB stream reports a corrupted size; used by tryDecompress which can produce large outputs.
findings.how_to_prove: Feed copy() a stream longer than Integer.MAX_VALUE bytes -> expected the true byte count, actual an overflowed (possibly negative) value; contrast with the long-based Reader/Writer overload.

findings.bug: append(Object,Object) stores any Object via Hashtable.put, but get() reads with Properties.getProperty, which returns null for any value that is not a String.
findings.why_real: java.util.Properties#getProperty casts only String values ('sval = (oval instanceof String) ? (String)oval : null'). Since append accepts Object value, a non-String value stored via append is silently lost on read.
findings.how_to_prove: new LocalFileMeta().append("k", 123L).get("k") -> expected 123L (or its retrievable value), actual null.

findings.bug: When the last element of the collection is null, a trailing separator is left in the output because the separator is appended for every non-null non-last element regardless of whether any later element is actually emitted.
findings.why_real: The separator is emitted inside 'if (objects[i] != null)' using 'i != size-1', but a trailing null element is skipped entirely, so the separator appended after the preceding element is never followed by content, producing a dangling delimiter.
findings.how_to_prove: StringUtils.join(Arrays.asList("a","b",null), ",") -> expected "a,b", actual "a,b,".

findings.bug: A group key whose last character is '%' (or has only one char after '%') triggers groupKey.charAt(++i) past the end, throwing StringIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of the intended IllegalArgumentException.
findings.why_real: The method is documented to reject malformed keys by throwing IllegalArgumentException('invalid groupkey'), and does so for other malformed cases; a dangling percent escape escapes that contract and surfaces an unrelated exception type.
findings.how_to_prove: GroupKey2.parseKey("dataId+group+ten%") -> expected IllegalArgumentException, actual StringIndexOutOfBoundsException.

findings.bug: merge() unconditionally adds the key to orderedKeys BEFORE calling super.merge(), but never removes it, so when the remapping function returns null (which removes the mapping) the key is left as a stale entry in orderedKeys.
findings.why_real: Hashtable/Properties.merge contract: if the remappingFunction returns null the mapping is removed (verified by running Properties.merge). orderedKeys must mirror the underlying map (it drives keys(), keySet(), entrySet(), forEach, toString); leaving a removed key desynchronizes the view from the map.
findings.how_to_prove: OrderedProperties p = new OrderedProperties(); p.put("k","v"); p.merge("k","x",(o,n)->null); Expected: p.containsKey("k")==false AND p.keySet() does not contain "k"; Actual: underlying map has no "k" (containsKey false) but p.keySet()/entrySet() still contains "k" (entrySet yields SimpleEntry("k", null)).

findings.bug: compute() only adds the key to orderedKeys when the result is non-null, but never removes the key from orderedKeys when compute removes an existing mapping (remapping returns null), leaving a stale key in orderedKeys.
findings.why_real: Hashtable/Properties.compute contract: if the remappingFunction returns null and a mapping existed, it is removed (verified by running Properties.compute). The override handles the add case but omits the removal case, so orderedKeys is left holding a key absent from the map.
findings.how_to_prove: OrderedProperties p = new OrderedProperties(); p.put("k2","v2"); p.compute("k2",(k,v)->null); Expected: p.keySet() and p.entrySet() do not contain "k2"; Actual: containsKey("k2")==false yet keySet()/entrySet() still list "k2" (entrySet gives SimpleEntry("k2", null)).

findings.bug: The case for "off" returns Boolean.TRUE instead of Boolean.FALSE.
findings.why_real: The method's own Javadoc says it supports 'on'/'off' pairs, and the sibling cases are consistent ("on"->TRUE, "no"->FALSE, '0'->FALSE, "false"->FALSE). "off" is a falsey token, so returning TRUE is a clear copy-paste defect (should be Boolean.FALSE).
findings.how_to_prove: assertEquals(Boolean.FALSE, StringUtils.toBoolean("off")); currently returns Boolean.TRUE. Also StringUtils.toBoolean("off", true) returns true instead of false.

findings.bug: The version segment is appended based on whether the GROUP is non-empty (isNotEmpty(group)) rather than whether the VERSION is non-empty, so a group-only service produces 'group/interface:null' and a version-only service silently drops its version.
findings.why_real: The canonical Dubbo service key format is group/interface:version. The append at line 916 uses the value of `version` but is guarded by isNotEmpty(group) (line 915) — an obvious copy-paste of the group guard on line 910. Correct guard is isNotEmpty(version).
findings.how_to_prove: Map m={GROUP_KEY:"g", INTERFACE_KEY:"com.I"} (no version) -> expected "g/com.I", actual "g/com.I:null". Map m2={INTERFACE_KEY:"com.I", VERSION_KEY:"1.0"} (no group) -> expected "com.I:1.0", actual "com.I" (version dropped).

findings.bug: randomSelectOne computes `int rate = originSize / cardinality` with no guard for cardinality == 0, throwing ArithmeticException (/ by zero) on a non-empty BitList whose elements all live in tailList.
findings.why_real: A BitList can be non-empty (size() > 0) while rootSet.cardinality() == 0: construct empty (rootSet unset) then addToTailList(e). size() = cardinality + tailSize > 0 makes randomSelectOne a legitimate call, but line 160 divides originSize by cardinality(0) before ever consulting tailList.
findings.how_to_prove: BitList<String> b = new BitList<>(new ArrayList<>(List.of("a")), true); b.addToTailList("x"); b.randomSelectOne(); -> throws ArithmeticException("/ by zero") instead of returning "x".

findings.bug: Deserialization assumes a single InputStream.read(bytes,0,length) call reads exactly `length` bytes and throws IllegalArgumentException when `read != length`, but InputStream.read is only contractually required to read *some* bytes (up to length), so a payload split across multiple reads (e.g. a network/chunked stream) fails spuriously.
findings.why_real: Per java.io.InputStream#read(byte[],int,int) Javadoc, the method reads 'up to len bytes' and 'may return fewer' even when more data will arrive; only readNBytes / DataInputStream.readFully guarantee a full read. Lines 96, 114, 153, and 197 all use the single-read pattern and reject any short read.
findings.how_to_prove: Wrap the JSONB bytes in an InputStream whose read(b,off,len) returns at most 1 byte per call (or a slow socket stream); readObject throws IllegalArgumentException("expected read length ... but actual read: 1") even though all bytes are ultimately available. A correct impl (readNBytes) returns the object.

findings.bug: The guard rejects only negative divisors (by < 0) but not zero, so divide(0) skips the check and executes bytes / 0, throwing ArithmeticException instead of the intended validation error.
findings.why_real: The exception message on line 222 reads 'divisor must be != 0', proving the author intended to reject zero; the comparison operator should be 'by <= 0'. As written, zero passes the guard and reaches 'bytes / by' (line 224) which throws java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero.
findings.how_to_prove: new MemorySize(1024L).divide(0) -> expected IllegalArgumentException('divisor must be != 0'), actual java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero.

findings.bug: skipFully loops on in.skip(len) and only breaks/throws when the return value is negative, but InputStream.skip() returns 0 (never negative) when it cannot skip more bytes, so at premature EOF the method spins forever instead of throwing IOException.
findings.why_real: The Javadoc promises 'IOException if it could not skip requested number of bytes for any reason (including EOF)'. Per the InputStream#skip contract the returned count is >= 0 and is 0 at EOF (e.g. ByteArrayInputStream.skip returns min(remaining,n)). The sibling readFully correctly checks ret < 0 because InputStream#read DOES return -1 at EOF; skipFully copied that guard even though skip never returns -1, so the ret < 0 branch is dead and the len -= ret loop never terminates.
findings.how_to_prove: IOUtils.skipFully(new ByteArrayInputStream(new byte[3]), 10) -> expected IOException('Premature EOF'), actual: infinite loop (skip() returns 3 then 0 forever, len stays at 7).

findings.bug: After loading a state machine by id, it caches the Item into the id-keyed map stateMachineMapById using a NAME_TENANT key (name+"_"+tenantId) instead of the id, so the id-map is polluted with a wrong-typed key and the name/tenant cache is never populated.
findings.why_real: The sibling method getStateMachine(name,tenant) at line 110 does the symmetric correct thing: it caches into the OTHER map (stateMachineMapById) using the id key (stateMachine.getId()). getStateMachineById should mirror that and put a name_tenant key into stateMachineMapByNameAndTenant, not into stateMachineMapById.
findings.how_to_prove: Configure a stateLangStore returning a StateMachine with id="m1", name="N", tenant="T". Call getStateMachineById("m1"). Assert stateMachineMapByNameAndTenant.containsKey("N_T") -> expected true, actual false; assert stateMachineMapById.containsKey("N_T") -> expected false, actual true.

findings.bug: encode() writes three trailing bytes (branchType, status code, lockStatus code at lines 385-388) but decode() only reads branchType and status and never reads the lockStatus byte, so a persisted/reloaded BranchSession always loses its lockStatus (silently defaults to Locked).
findings.why_real: encode() at lines 387-388 emits both status.getCode() and lockStatus.getCode(); a correct decode round-trip must consume both. decode() stops after status (line 546), leaving the lockStatus byte unread. GlobalSession.encode/decode is symmetric and reads every field it writes, establishing the round-trip contract.
findings.how_to_prove: Create BranchSession, setLockStatus(LockStatus.Rollbacking), encode() to bytes; new BranchSession().decode(bytes); assert getLockStatus()==Rollbacking -> expected Rollbacking, actual Locked.

findings.bug: On the incompatible-parameter-type error branch the log statement dereferences ret[i].getClass(), but ret[i] has never been assigned (still null) at that point, causing a NullPointerException instead of logging the offending value's class.
findings.why_real: Inside the branch guarded by (value != null && !parameterType.isAssignableFrom(value.getClass())), ret[i] has not yet been written (assignment only happens at line 99 in the else branch), so ret[i] is null and ret[i].getClass() throws NPE. The intended reference is value.getClass().
findings.how_to_prove: Invoke getArgValues so that getArgValue returns a value whose class is not assignable to the declared parameterType (e.g. declared type Integer, resolved value a String). Expected: error is logged and ret[i] set to null; actual: NullPointerException thrown from the LOGGER.error argument.

findings.bug: hash() calls instance.update(key.getBytes()) and then instance.digest(key.getBytes(UTF_8)); digest(input) performs a final update of input before digesting, so the SHA-256 is computed over key concatenated with itself (key||key) rather than over key.
findings.why_real: MessageDigest.digest(byte[] input) is documented to perform a final update with input then complete the hash. Combined with the preceding update(key), the digest input is key twice, which is not the plain SHA-256 of key. The correct pattern is a single update+digest() or digest(key) alone.
findings.how_to_prove: Compute reference = first 8 bytes of MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest("abc".getBytes(UTF_8)) folded to long; compare with SHA256Hash.hash("abc"). Expected equal; actual differs because the class hashes "abcabc".

findings.bug: compareTo computes (int)(this.startOffset - o.startOffset) on two longs, so the subtraction is truncated to int and can overflow, returning the wrong sign when the two start offsets differ by more than Integer.MAX_VALUE.
findings.why_real: startOffset is a long queue offset; the Comparable contract (and Collections.sort/TimSort) requires sgn(a.compareTo(b))==-sgn(b.compareTo(a)) and correct ordering. Verified with javac: (int)(0L - Long.MAX_VALUE) == 1 (should be negative), and (int)(3_000_000_000L - 0L) == -1294967296 (should be positive). Long-lived pop queues reach billions of offsets, so this truncation flips ordering for realistic values. The correct idiom is Long.compare(this.startOffset, o.startOffset).
findings.how_to_prove: PopCheckPoint a=new PopCheckPoint(); a.setStartOffset(0); PopCheckPoint b=new PopCheckPoint(); b.setStartOffset(Long.MAX_VALUE); assertTrue(a.compareTo(b) < 0) FAILS (returns +1). Also with b.setStartOffset(3_000_000_000L): a.compareTo(b) returns a negative number instead of positive, so Collections.sort of a list of checkpoints orders them backwards.

findings.bug: isTimeout() is missing the leading early-return guard, so when the timeout budget is already exhausted it still performs a spurious Thread.sleep(intervalMillis) before returning, instead of returning immediately.
findings.why_real: Upstream master isTimeout() begins with `if (timeoutMillis >= 0L && elapsedMillis >= timeoutMillis) { return true; }` which the reviewed version drops entirely; with timeoutMillis==0 upstream returns true with zero sleep, but this version sleeps intervalMillis first.
findings.how_to_prove: Construct new RetryExecutor(0L, 500L); call execute(x -> false, arg); measure wall-clock time: expected ~0ms (immediate timeout, no retry budget) per upstream semantics, but actual is >=500ms because isTimeout sleeps intervalMillis before evaluating the timeout. A test asserting the call returns in well under intervalMillis fails.

findings.bug: Every backslash escape in a Prometheus label value is decoded correctly by the if/else-if branches but then line 119 unconditionally re-appends the raw backslash + the escaped char, so the decoded value is corrupted (e.g. \" yields '"\"' and \n yields newline followed by literal '\n').
findings.why_real: The branches at lines 112-118 already append the intended unescaped character ('\\'->'\\', 'n'->newline, '"'->'"'); line 119 then appends '\\' and c again with no return/else, so both the decoded and the raw form land in labelvalue. Per the Prometheus text-format spec an escape sequence must produce exactly one decoded character. Sibling escape handlers in canonical parsers return after appending.
findings.how_to_prove: Feed a metric line with label value containing an escape, e.g. 'm{a="x\"y"} 1', through TextParser; expected label value 'x"y' but actual is 'x"\"y' (extra backslash-quote). A unit test on the parser output asserting equals('x"y') fails.

findings.bug: trim(str, ch) throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException when str consists entirely of ch and has length >= 2, because i advances past j and the computed length (j - i + 1) becomes negative.
findings.why_real: For input all equal to ch, the first loop leaves i == chars.length while the second loop stops at j == 0 (guard j > 0). Then new String(chars, i, j - i + 1) is called with a negative count; JLS/String(char[],int,int) throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException on count < 0. The method's contract (strip leading/trailing ch) implies it should return an empty string.
findings.how_to_prove: StringUtil.trim("aa", 'a') -> expected "" but actually throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException (offset=2, count=-1). Same for any all-'a' string of length>=2.

findings.bug: When the connect string starts with a comma, the code calls replace(",", "") which strips ALL commas, not just the leading one, so a valid multi-host string like ',h1:80,h2:81' is collapsed to 'h1:80h2:81' and then rejected as an invalid pattern.
findings.why_real: The guard connectString.startsWith(",") shows the clear intent to remove only the single leading comma; String.replace replaces every occurrence. The subsequent split(",") on the collapsed string yields one token 'h1:80h2:81', split(":") gives length 3 != 2, so ConnectStringParseException is thrown for input that is semantically valid.
findings.how_to_prove: ConnectUtils.parse(",127.0.0.1:80,127.0.0.2:81") -> expected 2 Address entries but actually throws ConnectStringParseException("Invalid connect string pattern.").

findings.bug: When computing the parent namespace's value-length limit for a gray (branch) namespace, the code fetches parentNamespace but then calls getItemValueLengthLimit(grayNamespace) instead of getItemValueLengthLimit(parentNamespace), so the parent's limit is never actually read.
findings.why_real: parentNamespace is fetched via findParentNamespace(grayNamespace) and null-checked precisely to consult its limit; the very next line ignores it and passes grayNamespace. getItemValueLengthLimit looks up overrides keyed by namespace id (namespace.getId()), and the gray namespace has a different id than the parent, so the parent's per-namespace override can never be found. This makes parentLimit == grayNamespaceLimit in the common case (both resolve to the gray namespace's own limit), so the branch parentLimit > grayNamespaceLimit is effectively dead and a gray namespace never inherits a larger parent limit as intended.
findings.how_to_prove: Configure namespaceValueLengthLimitOverride with parentNamespaceId -> 100 and leave the gray namespace at the default limit 20. Call checkItemValueLength on the gray namespace with a value of length 50. Expected (per the method's intent): allowed, because the parent limit 100 applies. Actual: BadRequestException 'value too long. length limit:20', because getItemValueLengthLimit(grayNamespace) returns 20 rather than the parent's 100.

findings.bug: Sizes the buffer with in.available() and does a single in.read(data) whose return value is ignored, so any stream where available() underreports or read() returns fewer bytes than requested yields a truncated/zero-padded, hence corrupted, Base64 result.
findings.why_real: InputStream Javadoc: available() is only an estimate of bytes that can be read without blocking (not the total length) and read(byte[]) reads 'up to' the array length and may read fewer bytes; correct code must loop until EOF (e.g. IOUtils.toByteArray/readAllBytes). The unused return value of read() proves the missing loop.
findings.how_to_prove: Wrap the image bytes in an InputStream whose read(byte[]) returns 1 byte per call (or whose available() reports fewer than the total). Expected: Base64 of the full image. Actual: buffer sized to the first available() value with only 1 byte filled and the rest left as 0x00, producing a wrong/truncated Base64 string.

findings.bug: The lock advertises reentrancy (支持重入) but keeps no hold count: tryLock() returns true again when the thread already holds the key, yet the first unlock() unconditionally DELs the key, so a single unlock releases a lock that was acquired multiple times.
findings.why_real: The class Javadoc states '支持重入' (supports reentrancy). A reentrant Lock must require as many unlock() calls as lock()/tryLock() successes (java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock contract). Here there is no counter; unlock() runs the DEL script on the first call and removes the ThreadLocal, breaking that contract.
findings.how_to_prove: With a mock StringRedisTemplate: thread A calls tryLock() (true), calls tryLock() again reentrantly (true), then unlock() once. Expected: A still holds the lock (a second thread's tryLock() must return false). Actual: the key is deleted after one unlock(), so another thread's tryLock() succeeds while A still believes it holds the lock.

findings.bug: setCredentialsProviderClassName assigns the given class name to the wrong field: it writes this.exceptionOverrideClassName instead of this.credentialsProviderClassName (copy-paste from setExceptionOverrideClassName).
findings.why_real: The field credentialsProviderClassName (declared line 77) is read by getCredentialsProviderClassName() (line 878) but is never assigned anywhere; line 893 instead clobbers exceptionOverrideClassName. Compare the sibling setExceptionOverrideClassName (line 946) which correctly assigns exceptionOverrideClassName, and setDriverClassName which assigns its own field. So after calling this setter the getter for the intended property returns null AND an unrelated property is corrupted.
findings.how_to_prove: HikariConfig c = new HikariConfig(); c.setCredentialsProviderClassName("com.zaxxer.hikari.pool.TestCredentialsProvider"); assertEquals("com.zaxxer.hikari.pool.TestCredentialsProvider", c.getCredentialsProviderClassName()); // expected: that class name, actual: null. Also assertNull(c.getExceptionOverrideClassName()); // expected: null, actual: the credentials-provider class name (corrupted).

findings.bug: Deprecation-warning version guard uses '>= 1' on String.compareTo, so the warning is NOT emitted for the exact version 4.3.6 even though the message and intent say 'Hibernate 4.3.6 and newer'.
findings.why_real: For version string "4.3.6", substring(0,5).compareTo("4.3.6") returns 0, and 0 >= 1 is false, so the branch is skipped. compareTo returns a sign (negative/zero/positive), not increments of 1, so the only correct threshold for 'this version or newer' is '>= 0'. The immediately-following log message explicitly claims coverage of '4.3.6 and newer', contradicting the guard.
findings.how_to_prove: If Version.getVersionString() returns "4.3.6", constructing HikariConnectionProvider should log the deprecation warning; with '>= 1' it does not. Expected: warning logged for 4.3.6; actual: not logged (only logged for versions lexicographically greater, e.g. 4.3.7).

findings.bug: trimToSize dereferences toRemove.size without a null check, but put(key, null) stores a literal null map value (line 140), so evicting such an entry throws NullPointerException.
findings.why_real: The class Javadoc for put (lines 118-124) explicitly documents putting a null item as a SUPPORTED input that 'will result in an entry remaining in the cache with a null value and 0 size' and that 'onItemEvicted may be called with the given key and a null value'; yet trimToSize does final Entry<Y> toRemove = last.getValue(); currentSize -= toRemove.size; with no null guard, so when that null-valued eldest entry is evicted, toRemove is null and toRemove.size NPEs.
findings.how_to_prove: new LruCache<String,Object>(2){}; cache.put("a", null); then cache.put("b", new Object()); cache.put("c", new Object()); (each real item size 1, currentSize reaches 2 then eviction triggers). Expected: eldest key "a" evicted cleanly. Actual: NullPointerException at trimToSize line 186 because the stored value for "a" is null.

findings.bug: Guard uses itemSize >= maxSize, rejecting an item whose size exactly equals maxSize, but the documented contract is to reject only items strictly larger than the cache size.
findings.why_real: The put Javadoc (lines 109-111) states 'If the size of the item is larger than the total cache size, the item will not be added to the cache'; 'larger than' means strictly greater (>), whereas the code uses >=, so an item of size == maxSize is incorrectly rejected and onItemEvicted is called instead of caching it.
findings.how_to_prove: LruCache<String,Object> c = new LruCache<>(1); c.put("k", value) where getSize(value)==1 (default). Expected per Javadoc: item cached (size not larger than 1). Actual: itemSize(1) >= maxSize(1) is true, onItemEvicted fired and item not added; c.get("k") returns null.

findings.bug: equals dereferences first.equals(...) and second.equals(...) without null checks, so an instance built with the public no-arg constructor (which leaves first/second null) throws NullPointerException when compared.
findings.why_real: The no-arg constructor is public and documented to 'leave them null'; hashCode (line 68) also calls first.hashCode() unconditionally. Both violate the Object.equals/hashCode contract of not throwing for a validly-constructed instance; sibling handling of 'third' correctly uses Util.bothNullOrEqual (line 59), showing the null-safe pattern that first/second omit.
findings.how_to_prove: new MultiClassKey().equals(new MultiClassKey(String.class, Integer.class)). Expected: false (not equal). Actual: NullPointerException at line 53 because this.first is null.

findings.bug: A malformed numeric XML entity such as "&#;" (entity string "#") reaches unescapeEntity and does e.charAt(1) / Integer.parseInt on an empty or non-numeric substring, throwing an unguarded StringIndexOutOfBoundsException or NumberFormatException instead of a JSONException.
findings.why_real: The method's own design intent is graceful handling: for an unknown alphabetic entity it re-encodes and returns '&'+e+';' (lines 139-143) rather than throwing, and nextEntity(...) signals malformed entities via syntaxError(JSONException). The numeric '#' branch violates that contract by dereferencing e.charAt(1) when e.length()==1 and by feeding empty/invalid text to Integer.parseInt, so valid-to-reach but malformed markup crashes with the wrong (unchecked) exception type instead of a JSONException.
findings.how_to_prove: Call XMLTokener.unescapeEntity("#") (or parse XML content containing "&#;", e.g. via nextContent on input "a&#;b"): expected a JSONException (or graceful passthrough) but actual is java.lang.StringIndexOutOfBoundsException from e.charAt(1); similarly unescapeEntity("#x") yields Integer.parseInt("") -> NumberFormatException.

findings.bug: A logically-empty map (size()==0) still yields a phantom entry when iterated: after all keys are removed, iteration from Integer.MIN_VALUE returns one node with content==null.
findings.why_real: deleteNode's two-children path (lines 1087-1101) leaves the deleted node as a permanent tombstone (content=null, tombstonesCount++), and never physically removes it. nodesIteratorAt switches on the RAW field this.size (line 414), which still counts tombstones, so a map holding exactly one tombstone dispatches to the size==1 iterator branch (lines 437-478). That branch does NOT filter tombstones: its next() returns true and getCurrOffset() returns theOnlyNode.offset while getCurrValue() returns null. size() (line 408) correctly returns 0, so size() and iteration contradict each other.
findings.how_to_prove: put(36),put(28),put(127),put(45); then removeAt(36),removeAt(127),removeAt(45),removeAt(28). Expected: size()==0 and nodesIteratorAt(Integer.MIN_VALUE).next()==false (empty). Actual: size()==0 but the iterator yields one entry offset=36, value=null. Verified by compiling the class and running this sequence.

findings.bug: Deleting an internal node whose in-order successor has a left child never physically removes the node; it is only marked as a tombstone, so removeAt cannot ever truly empty a tree of such shape and dead nodes accumulate as the map root.
findings.why_real: The standard red-black successor-splice path is commented out (lines 1084-1086) and replaced by a tombstone fallback (lines 1087-1101) guarded by 'if (y.left.isNotSentinel())'. The author's own FIXME at line 1087 ('standard rb-tree removal strategy cannot be applied, just mark z as tombstone for now') and lines 1147-1148 ('this does happen apparently, so we need another removal strategy') confirm the offset-fixup invariant (lines 1142-1150) is violated for real inputs.
findings.how_to_prove: put(36),put(28),put(127),put(45) builds a tree where 36 is the root with two children and successor 127 has a left child 45. removeAt(36) leaves the root node in place with content=null (visible via collect(): '[36 as 36] null'); the tree still has this node after removeAt(127),removeAt(45),removeAt(28). Expected a physically empty tree; actual is a residual tombstone root.

findings.bug: escapeXmlElementName("") throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException on escapedName.charAt(0) when the element name is empty; this is reachable from exportRow via column.getName() and from printHeader via getSource().getName() with no empty-name guard.
findings.why_real: replaceAll on an empty string returns an empty string, and charAt(0) on "" throws (verified: 'Index 0 out of bounds for length 0'). exportRow (line 105) passes column.getName() directly with no CommonUtils.isEmpty fallback, unlike printHeader which only guards the label path (lines 81-83) but still calls escapeXmlElementName(columns[i].getName()) unguarded at line 91, and escapes getSource().getName() unguarded at line 73. An empty/unnamed result column or unnamed source therefore crashes the whole XML export.
findings.how_to_prove: Call escapeXmlElementName("") (or export a result set whose column getName() returns an empty string). Expected: a valid element name such as "_". Actual: java.lang.StringIndexOutOfBoundsException at line 175.

findings.bug: The fractional-seconds branch rigidly reads exactly 3 digits (parseInt(date, offset += 1, offset += 3)), so it rejects valid ISO-8601 timestamps whose fractional part has other than 3 digits.
findings.why_real: ISO-8601 (and the class Javadoc format [.sss]) permit a variable number of fractional-second digits; the reader hard-codes 3. For a 1-digit fraction '2018-06-25T12:00:00.1Z' parseInt is called with beginIndex=20,endIndex=23 on a length-22 string, so endIndex>value.length() throws NumberFormatException (an IllegalArgumentException) which is caught and rethrown as ParseException->JsonParseException. For >3 digits like '...00.123456Z' it consumes only '123' and then treats the remaining digit as the timezone indicator, throwing IndexOutOfBoundsException('Invalid time zone indicator 4').
findings.how_to_prove: new Gson with UtcDateTypeAdapter registered for Date; gson.fromJson("\"2018-06-25T12:00:00.1Z\"", Date.class). Expected: a Date at 2018-06-25T12:00:00.100Z. Actual: JsonParseException wrapping ParseException 'Failed to parse date'. Same failure for the valid input "2018-06-25T12:00:00.123456Z".

findings.bug: hasSubscriberForEvent always walks the full event-class hierarchy (lookupAllEventTypes) even when eventInheritance is disabled, so it can return true for an event that post() will deliver to zero subscribers.
findings.why_real: post()/postSingleEvent() only consult superclasses/interfaces when eventInheritance is true (line 389-398); when false it uses the exact eventClass only. hasSubscriberForEvent (line 369) never checks the eventInheritance flag, contradicting the documented behavior of eventInheritance(false) which turns off hierarchy consideration.
findings.how_to_prove: Build EventBus.builder().eventInheritance(false).build(); register a subscriber for a super type (or interface) Base; post a Sub instance (Sub extends Base). Assert post delivers to 0 subscribers (correct) but hasSubscriberForEvent(Sub.class) returns true -> expected false, actual true.

findings.bug: On the InterruptedException path the executorRunning flag is reset to false in an unsynchronized finally block, so a concurrent enqueue that observed executorRunning==true (and therefore skipped submitting a new task) can leave a queued PendingPost with no running executor, delaying delivery until the next enqueue.
findings.why_real: enqueue() reads/writes executorRunning only inside synchronized(this) (lines 39-45); the normal drain exit (lines 55-61) also resets it inside synchronized. The finally at line 70 resets it OUTSIDE the lock, breaking the invariant that executorRunning transitions happen under the monitor and creating a lost-wakeup window (fixed upstream by resetting the flag inside a synchronized block).
findings.how_to_prove: Interrupt the executor thread while it is in queue.poll(1000) so InterruptedException fires; concurrently call enqueue() in the window after the loop breaks but before the finally runs (enqueue sees executorRunning still true, skips submit); after finally sets it false the pending event is never dispatched. Deterministic repro requires instrumenting the poll to signal the interrupt/enqueue interleaving.

findings.bug: values().get(index) returns kvpairs[index*2], which is the KEY at that pair, not the value; the value lives at kvpairs[index*2 + 1].
findings.why_real: The constructor stores key at even index (i++) then value at the following odd index (i++), so pair p occupies kvpairs[2p]=key and kvpairs[2p+1]=value; get(), containsKey() and the entrySet iterator all read value at odd offsets. The values() override reads the even (key) slot, contradicting these sibling methods and the Map#values contract.
findings.how_to_prove: PackedMap.of(new LinkedHashMap(){{put("k","v");}}).values().iterator().next() -> expected "v" but returns "k"; for a map {a=1,b=2} values() yields [a,b] instead of [1,2].

findings.bug: The \uXXXX escape decodes the four hex digits with byte-wide shifts (24,16,8,0) instead of nibble-wide shifts (12,8,4,0), so a 4-hex-digit unicode escape is decoded to the wrong character.
findings.why_real: Each hex digit is a 4-bit nibble; a 16-bit char is built from 4 nibbles shifted by 12,8,4,0. Shifting by 24/16/8/0 treats each digit as a full byte, which is incorrect (and the Jetty original this file is copied from uses 12,8,4). convertHexDigit returns 0-15, so the result is a garbage code point.
findings.how_to_prove: QuotedStringTokenizer.unquote("\"\\u0041\"") -> expected "A" (0x0041) but returns char (0<<24)+(0<<16)+(4<<8)+1 = 0x0401 = 'Ё'.

findings.bug: skip() returns the raw result of read(), which is -1 at end of stream, violating InputStream#skip which must never return a negative value.
findings.why_real: InputStream#skip javadoc: 'returns the actual number of bytes skipped, which might be zero' and is always >= 0. read(byte[],int,int) returns -1 at EOF, and skip forwards that value directly, so skip returns -1 at EOF.
findings.how_to_prove: new FlightRecorderInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(new byte[0])).skip(10) -> expected 0 but returns -1.

findings.bug: failedThenRestarted() indexes histories.get(size-2) without a size guard, throwing IndexOutOfBoundsException when the state has fewer than 2 histories.
findings.why_real: The sibling method isResumingAfterPause() (line 225) does the identical size-2 lookup but first guards with 'this.histories.size() < 2 -> return false'; failedThenRestarted() omits that guard. The public constructor new State(Type.RESTARTED) yields current==RESTARTED with exactly one history, so the current==RESTARTED guard is insufficient.
findings.how_to_prove: new State(State.Type.RESTARTED).failedThenRestarted() -> expected: returns false (like isResumingAfterPause), actual: IndexOutOfBoundsException from histories.get(-1).

findings.bug: On a key conflict (an existing non-Map value at an intermediate path segment) the code 'continue's only the current level instead of skipping the whole entry, so it injects a spurious sibling branch rather than ignoring the conflicting key as its log message claims.
findings.why_real: The warning message states 'Conflict at key ... ignoring it', i.e. the whole flattened key should be dropped. But 'continue' only skips assigning currentMap for that one segment; the loop proceeds with the remaining segments against the parent map, creating bogus top-level keys. The lastKey branch (line 212) is the correct 'skip the whole entry' model that this branch fails to follow.
findings.how_to_prove: flattenToNestedMap(Map.of("a",1,"a.b.c",2)) -> expected {a=1} (a.b.c ignored due to conflict on 'a'), actual {a=1, b={c=2}} (spurious 'b' branch created).

findings.bug: When constructed with an explicit statusCodes list, process() raises an error for every response whose code is NOT in the list, so successful responses (e.g. 200) are treated as failures.
findings.why_real: For a class named FailedResponseInterceptor whose default mode raises on code>=400, the statusCodes list represents codes to treat as failures; the guard '!statusCodes.contains(code)' inverts that, firing on all codes except the listed ones. A 200 response with statusCodes=[500] triggers raiseError.
findings.how_to_prove: new FailedResponseInterceptor(List.of(500)).process(response(200), null, ctx) -> expected: no exception (200 is a success, not one of the failure codes), actual: HttpClientResponseException thrown because !contains(200).

findings.bug: The path escape function replaces '/' with '~/' but never escapes a literal '~', so a group whose name ends in '~' is indistinguishable from the '~/' escape sequence and splitPath merges it with the following segment.
findings.why_real: Round-trip contract: buildGroupPath(escape=true) then splitPath must reproduce the original segments. splitPath uses the regex (?<!~)/ which treats any '/' preceded by '~' as escaped. Because escapeGroupNameForPath does not double/escape the escape char '~', a real trailing '~' collides with the escape marker, breaking the inverse relationship of escapeGroupNameForPath/unescapeGroupNameForPath.
findings.how_to_prove: buildGroupPath(true, "a~", "b") -> "/a~/b"; splitPath("/a~/b", true) expected {"a~","b"} but actual returns a single element {"a/b"} (the '/' before 'b' is treated as escaped and then unescaped to '/'). Two distinct groups collapse into one.

findings.bug: formatAddress(InetAddress) compresses even a single 16-bit zero field into '::', producing non-RFC-5952 (and ambiguous) output.
findings.why_real: The Javadoc of formatAddress states it formats IPv6 'according to RFC5952 rules', and RFC 5952 section 4.2.2 says '::' MUST NOT shorten just one 16-bit 0 field. compactLongestZeroSequence fills any best run of length >= 1 with -1 and formatAddress6 emits '::' for it. The sibling method canonize does this correctly, guarding with 'maxZeroGroupLength <= 1'.
findings.how_to_prove: Take the Inet6Address for 2001:db8:0:1:1:1:1:1 (single zero group at index 2) and call NetworkUtils.formatAddress(inet). Expected per RFC 5952: 2001:db8:0:1:1:1:1:1 (no '::'); actual: 2001:db8::1:1:1:1:1.

findings.bug: getIat() returns a nullable Long and is auto-unboxed via getIat() + 1, throwing NullPointerException when the token has no iat claim.
findings.why_real: iat is a protected Long that is null unless set/deserialized; the JWT 'iat' claim is optional per RFC 7519. Sibling accessors (isExpired, isNotBefore) explicitly null-check exp/nbf before use, but isIssuedBeforeSessionStart does not, so 'getIat() + 1' unboxes null.
findings.how_to_prove: new JsonWebToken().isIssuedBeforeSessionStart(1000L) -> expected a boolean (e.g. treat missing iat gracefully) but actual throws NullPointerException at getIat() + 1.

findings.bug: Bounds guard uses 'vertexNum > getVertexCount()' so vertexNum == getVertexCount() passes the check, then vertices[2*vertexNum] reads one element past the end of the array.
findings.why_real: getVertexCount() returns localVertices.length/2, so a valid max index is count-1; the sibling setVertex correctly rejects with '> localVertices.length/2 - 1'. Passing vertexNum == count accesses vertices[length] which throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
findings.how_to_prove: new Polygon(new float[]{0,0,1,0,0,1}).getVertex(3, new Vector2()) -> expected IllegalArgumentException 'vertex 3 doesn't exist', actual ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException on vertices[6].

findings.bug: contains(node, identity=false) iterates the entire backing 'nodes' array (capacity length) instead of only the first 'size' elements, so it calls other.equals(node) on the null trailing slots.
findings.why_real: nodes is allocated to capacity and trailing entries beyond 'size' are null; every other size-bounded method (pop/down/equals/hashCode/toString) loops to 'size'. Calling null.equals(node) throws NullPointerException on valid input.
findings.how_to_prove: BinaryHeap h = new BinaryHeap(16,false); h.add(new BinaryHeap.Node(1)); h.contains(new BinaryHeap.Node(2), false) -> expected false, actual NullPointerException at nodes[1].equals(...).

findings.bug: Uses strict '>' and '<' for the containment test, so an identical rectangle (or any edge-touching sub-rectangle) is reported as NOT contained.
findings.why_real: Sibling overloads contains(float,float) (line 189) and contains(Circle) (line 201) use inclusive '<='/'>=' boundaries. A rectangle is geometrically contained in itself, so the inclusive semantics of the other overloads should apply; the strict comparison is inconsistent with them.
findings.how_to_prove: new Rectangle(0,0,10,10).contains(new Rectangle(0,0,10,10)) -> expected true, actual false (xmin>x is 0>0 == false).

findings.bug: getSetterType() throws NullPointerException (not the intended ReflectionException) when the property has no setter, because it calls setTypes.get(propertyName).getValue() on a possibly-null Entry.
findings.why_real: The sibling method getGetterType() (line 424-430) does exactly the same job but correctly uses getTypes.getOrDefault(propertyName, nullEntry).getValue() so it can reach and throw the 'There is no setter/getter for property' ReflectionException. getSetterType() omits the getOrDefault, so setTypes.get(missing) returns null and .getValue() NPEs before the guard on line 404 can run. Additionally the error message on line 405 interpolates the local 'clazz' (which is null in that branch) instead of the class field, so even when reachable it prints 'in null'.
findings.how_to_prove: new Reflector(SomeBean.class).getSetterType("doesNotExist") -> expected: ReflectionException with 'There is no setter for property named doesNotExist'; actual: NullPointerException at setTypes.get(propertyName).getValue().

findings.bug: getType("paramN") resolves the generic name by names.get(N-1), treating N-1 as a Map key, but 'names' is a SortedMap keyed by the real parameter position which skips special parameters (RowBounds/ResultHandler); the generic names paramN are actually assigned by ordinal position, not by key, so getType returns the wrong type (or null) whenever a special parameter precedes a real one.
findings.why_real: getNamedParams() (lines 168-177) builds the generic names by iterating names.entrySet() and assigning param1, param2... using the ordinal counter i (0->param1), NOT the map key. But getType() maps param1 to names.get(0) i.e. map key 0. For a method like aMethod(RowBounds rb, int a) the map is {1 -> "0"} (key 1, per the class Javadoc example on line 61), so param1 must mean the sole real parameter, yet names.get(0) returns null and getType yields null. The two methods disagree on what paramN means.
findings.how_to_prove: For mapper method List<X> m(RowBounds rb, @Param x String a): resolver.getType("param1") -> expected String type; actual null because names.get(0) is null (the only key is 1).

findings.bug: For a generic CharSequence (not String/AsciiString) the trim returns c.subSequence(start, end) where end is the INCLUSIVE index of the last non-space char, but CharSequence.subSequence's end parameter is EXCLUSIVE. This drops the last character of the trimmed result.
findings.why_real: The sibling instance method AsciiString#trim() (line 1007-1019) computes the same inclusive 'end' and correctly converts it to a length via 'end - start + 1' when constructing the result. The static generic branch instead passes the inclusive 'end' directly as the exclusive end of subSequence, so it is off by one and truncates the last kept char. CharSequence.subSequence(start,end) is specified with end exclusive.
findings.how_to_prove: Pass a non-String, non-AsciiString CharSequence, e.g. StringBuilder sb=new StringBuilder(" ab "); AsciiString.trim(sb). Expected "ab"; actual "a". Also new StringBuilder("ab ") -> expected "ab", actual "a".

findings.bug: When limit == 0 the method returns 0 instead of returning the 'initial' seed value.
findings.why_real: A reduction over zero elements must yield the initial value. The interface default implementation of weakPeekReduce (line 86-90) documents and returns 'initial' as the extreme weak case, and the Javadoc says the method returns 'the last result of the reduction operation' (which for zero processed elements is 'initial'). Returning the hard-coded 0 contradicts both the default impl and the contract for any non-zero initial.
findings.how_to_prove: MpscIntQueue q = MpscIntQueue.create(8, -1); int r = q.weakPeekReduce(0, 42, (a,b)->a+b); Expected 42; actual 0.

findings.bug: Bounds check uses 'if (index > pos)' instead of 'if (index < 0 || index >= pos)'. charAt(pos) does not throw and instead reads chars[pos], which is outside the logical length (returns a stale/uninitialized char) whenever pos < chars.length; a negative index is also not validated.
findings.why_real: The CharSequence contract requires charAt to throw IndexOutOfBoundsException when index is negative or >= length(). Here length() == pos, so charAt(pos) must throw but instead returns the raw backing-array element at index pos (e.g. '�' from the unused tail of the doubled buffer). length() returns pos, confirming the valid index range is [0, pos).
findings.how_to_prove: AppendableCharSequence s = new AppendableCharSequence(16); s.append('a'); // pos=1, chars.length=16. s.charAt(1) is expected to throw IndexOutOfBoundsException (index == length()) but returns '�'.

findings.bug: The bounds check 'if (start > pos || length > pos)' fails to reject end > pos when start >= 1. e.g. start=2,end=4,pos=3 passes (length=2<=3, start=2<=3) and reads chars[3] which is past the logical content.
findings.why_real: substring is documented to create a String 'from the given start to end' of the logical sequence whose length is pos. The correct guard must reject end > pos (i.e. start + length > pos), as done implicitly by String.substring. The current check only limits start and length individually, allowing reads of uninitialized/stale tail bytes instead of throwing IndexOutOfBoundsException.
findings.how_to_prove: AppendableCharSequence s = new AppendableCharSequence(16); s.append('a'); s.append('b'); s.append('c'); // pos=3, chars.length=16. s.substring(2,4) is expected to throw IndexOutOfBoundsException (end 4 > length 3) but returns "c�".

findings.symbol: HttpObjectDecoder static init of ISO_CONTROL_OR_WHITESPACE / LATIN_WHITESPACE
findings.bug: The classification tables are populated with `for (byte b = Byte.MIN_VALUE; b < Byte.MAX_VALUE; b++)`, which stops at 126 and never sets the entry for b == 127 (0x7F, DEL). Thus ISO_CONTROL_OR_WHITESPACE[128+127] stays false even though DEL is an ISO control char, so isControlOrWhitespaceAsciiChar((byte)0x7F) wrongly returns false.
findings.why_real: Character.isISOControl(0x7F) is true (0x7F is a C0 control, DEL). The table is intended to mark all control/whitespace bytes; every other control byte is marked. The loop bound `< Byte.MAX_VALUE` is an off-by-one that leaves index 127 unset. Consequence: in splitInitialLine() the trailing-byte guard (line 1072-1083) fails to reject a request/response line ending in DEL, and skipLineChars treats DEL inconsistently — a control character leaks through where the code clearly intends to flag it.
findings.how_to_prove: Feed the request-line bytes 'GET / HTTP/1.1\x7f\r\n' to HttpRequestDecoder. Expected (matching how other control chars like 0x1f are handled): an IllegalArgumentException 'Illegal character in request line' via splitInitialLine's lastByte guard. Actual: no exception is raised for the trailing 0x7F because isControlOrWhitespaceAsciiChar(0x7F) returns false. A direct unit test: assert HttpObjectDecoder's isControlOrWhitespaceAsciiChar((byte)0x7f) — reachable via the same table — is expected true but is false.

findings.bug: valueOfHelper returns values[b & 0xFF] and only catches ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException; for an index that is in array bounds but never populated (a gap in the sparse VALUES table), it returns null instead of throwing. Every sibling valueOf in the codebase (MqttConnectReturnCode.valueOf, MqttProperties.MqttPropertyType.valueOf) null-checks and throws IllegalArgumentException; this one does not.
findings.why_real: The VALUES arrays are sparse: e.g. SubAck VALUES has length 163 but only indices 0,1,2,128,131,135,143,145,151,158,161,162 are filled, so index 3 is null. MqttDecoder.decodeSubackPayload builds List<Integer> and calls new MqttSubAckPayload(Iterable<Integer>), which invokes MqttReasonCodes.SubAck.valueOf(v.byteValue()). A SUBACK carrying an undefined-but-in-range reason-code byte (e.g. 0x03) causes list.add(null). The supposedly-typed List<MqttReasonCodes.SubAck> then holds null, and any subsequent MqttSubAckPayload.reasonCodes()/grantedQoSLevels() (also called by MqttEncoder.encodeSubAckMessage) dereferences code.byteValue() -> NullPointerException. Contract: sibling valueOf methods reject unknown codes with IllegalArgumentException; this silently yields null. Confirmed empirically that VALUES[3] is null.
findings.how_to_prove: MqttReasonCodes.SubAck.valueOf((byte) 0x03): expected IllegalArgumentException (as MqttConnectReturnCode.valueOf throws for unknown codes), actual returns null. End-to-end: decode a SUBACK whose payload granted-code byte is 0x03, then call payload.grantedQoSLevels() -> expected a value or a clean decode failure, actual NullPointerException on code.byteValue().

findings.bug: MqttProperty.equals compares value via this.value.equals(that.value) and hashCode uses value.hashCode(); BinaryProperty's value is a byte[], so equals/hashCode use array identity, not content. Two BinaryProperty instances with identical propertyId and identical byte content are not equal and (almost always) hash differently.
findings.why_real: BinaryProperty (CORRELATION_DATA 0x09, AUTHENTICATION_DATA 0x16) does not override equals/hashCode, so it inherits the base implementation that calls value.equals()/value.hashCode() on a byte[] — which is Object identity for arrays, violating the value-object equals contract that sibling properties (StringProperty, IntegerProperty) satisfy. A decode of two packets with identical correlation data yields BinaryProperty objects that are not equal, breaking property/collection comparisons and round-trip equality checks.
findings.how_to_prove: new MqttProperties.BinaryProperty(CORRELATION_DATA, new byte[]{1,2,3}).equals(new MqttProperties.BinaryProperty(CORRELATION_DATA, new byte[]{1,2,3})): expected true (equal propertyId and content), actual false; hashCode() of the two also differ. Contrast with StringProperty of equal content which returns true.

findings.bug: When a valid 5-byte protobuf varint32 length field is delivered split so that exactly 4 bytes are currently in the buffer (all four with the continuation bit set), readRawVarint40 throws CorruptedFrameException("malformed varint.") instead of waiting for the 5th byte.
findings.why_real: readRawVarint32 routes to readRawVarint40 only when firstOneOnStop == 0, i.e. all four buffered bytes have the high (continuation) bit set. That is exactly the prefix of a legal 5-byte varint (values with bit>=28 set, e.g. any frame length >= 0x10000000, which is representable since maxFrameLength defaults to Integer.MAX_VALUE and ProtobufVarint32LengthFieldPrepender.computeRawVarint32Size returns 5 for such lengths). The condition `buffer.readableBytes() == 4` on line 143 means the 5th (terminating) byte has simply not arrived yet. A ByteToMessageDecoder can be handed exactly 4 bytes and then more later, so this is valid, incomplete input. The correct behavior is the same as every other incomplete-varint path in this class (readRawVarint24 resets and returns 0, and decode() then leaves readerIndex unchanged so it retries on the next read). Instead readRawVarint40 throws, and the exception propagates out of decode() to the pipeline as an exceptionCaught, aborting decoding of a perfectly valid stream. The sibling `> 4` branch on the same line correctly reads getByte(readerIndex+4) and only throws when that 5th byte itself has the continuation bit set (a genuinely malformed >5-byte varint), confirming the == 4 case is meant to be 'need more data', not 'malformed'.
findings.how_to_prove: Encode a body whose length needs a 5-byte varint (>= 0x10000000). Take the 5-byte length prefix L[0..4] (L[0..3] each have 0x80 set, L[4] is the terminating byte). Feed only the first 4 bytes L[0..3] to an EmbeddedChannel with ProtobufVarint32FrameDecoder: expected -> decoder produces no output and leaves readerIndex unchanged (waits for more); actual -> throws CorruptedFrameException("malformed varint."). Equivalent direct unit test: ProtobufVarint32FrameDecoder.readRawVarint32(Unpooled.wrappedBuffer(new byte[]{(byte)0xFF,(byte)0xFF,(byte)0xFF,(byte)0xFF})) throws instead of leaving readerIndex at 0.

findings.bug: The minimum-length guard is `readable < 3`, but decoding needs 4 bytes (3-digit code + 1 separator). A 3-byte line makes parseCode() consume all 3 bytes and then `frame.readByte()` on line 58 throws IndexOutOfBoundsException.
findings.why_real: parseCode() reads exactly 3 bytes; line 58 unconditionally reads a 4th (the separator). The guard should be `readable < 4`. A line that is exactly a 3-char code with no separator/text (e.g. server sends "250\r\n") passes the guard and crashes with a raw IOOBE instead of the intended DecoderException produced by newDecoderException(). The off-by-one is in the bound: the code contractually requires code(3)+separator(1).
findings.how_to_prove: Feed the decoder the bytes "250\r\n". LineBasedFrameDecoder (stripDelimiter=true) yields a 3-byte frame "250". Expected: a clean DecoderException("Received invalid line..."). Actual: IndexOutOfBoundsException from frame.readByte() at line 58 (wrapped by ByteToMessageDecoder into a DecoderException whose cause is IOOBE).

findings.bug: parseNumber() returns Character.digit(...) which is -1 for any non-digit byte, and parseCode() never validates the result. Non-digit code characters silently produce a wrong numeric code (or a negative one), instead of being rejected as an invalid line.
findings.why_real: For input like "2X0 ok", digit('X')=-1, so code = 200 + (-1*10) + 0 = 190 — an in-range but completely wrong code, returned as a valid DefaultSmtpResponse with NO error (silent data corruption). For input like "XYZ ok", code = -100-10-1 = -111, which then makes the DefaultSmtpResponse constructor throw IllegalArgumentException("code must be 100 <= code <= 599") rather than the decoder's intended DecoderException. A response-code parser must reject non-digit characters; here it does not.
findings.how_to_prove: Input "2X0 ok\r\n": expected a DecoderException (invalid code), actual is DefaultSmtpResponse with code()==190. Input "XYZ ok\r\n": expected DecoderException("Received invalid line"), actual is an IllegalArgumentException from the DefaultSmtpResponse constructor (wrapped as DecoderException with the wrong message/cause).

findings.bug: newDecoderException is called with `readerIndex`/`readable` taken from `frame` (lines 52-53) but reads from the raw `buffer` argument: `buffer.toString(readerIndex, readable, ...)`. Because frame is a readRetainedSlice, its readerIndex is 0 (slice-relative) while buffer's readerIndex has already advanced past the consumed line, so the diagnostic string is read from the wrong region of the wrong buffer.
findings.why_real: The error message is supposed to echo the invalid line. frame's slice-relative index 0 does not correspond to the invalid line's position in buffer (buffer.readerIndex has moved forward by the line length after super.decode). The method should call `frame.toString(...)` using frame's own content, not `buffer`. The result is a misleading/garbage error message (and, if buffer capacity were smaller, could even IOOBE).
findings.how_to_prove: Feed an invalid separator, e.g. "250!text\r\n" (separator '!' hits the default branch -> newDecoderException). Expected message contains "250!text"; actual message contains whatever bytes sit at buffer offset [0, readable), which is not the line just decoded.

findings.bug: contentLength is a long parsed from the content-length header, but remainingLength is computed as `(int)(contentLength - alreadyReadChunkSize)`. For a declared content-length > Integer.MAX_VALUE the cast overflows to a negative value, which then flows into readBytes(...) as a negative length.
findings.why_real: getContentLength() accepts any non-negative long (only rejects < 0). The sibling StompSubframeAggregator#isContentLengthInvalid deliberately guards the same value with `Math.min(Integer.MAX_VALUE, getLong(...))`, showing the intended contract that content-length must be clamped before use as an int. The decoder omits this clamp: with contentLength = 3_000_000_000, remainingLength becomes negative, toRead is set negative, and readBytes throws IllegalArgumentException, turning a (large but structurally valid) header into a decode failure via the wrong path.
findings.how_to_prove: Send a STOMP frame with header "content-length:3000000000" followed by body bytes and NUL. Expected: content is read/chunked according to maxChunkSize (or a clean 'too large' rejection). Actual: (int)(3000000000L) overflows to -1294967296, toRead goes negative, and readBytes(ctx.alloc(), in, negative) throws IllegalArgumentException, producing a BAD_FRAME error subframe.

findings.bug: isEquals() encodes two ByteBufs but its finally block calls valueBuf.readableBytes()/oldValueBuf.readableBytes() (no-op int getters) instead of release(), so both encoded buffers are leaked on every call.
findings.why_real: encode() returns freshly-allocated Netty ByteBufs that must be released; the sibling method sizeAsync() in the same class (line 146) correctly calls buf.release() after encoding, and readableBytes() has no reference-count side effect, so the finally block clearly intended release(). isEquals is invoked by compareAndSetAsync (lines 250 and 260), leaking 2 buffers per compare-and-set.
findings.how_to_prove: Wrap an RTransaction bucket over a pooled/leak-detecting ByteBufAllocator, call bucket.compareAndSet(expect, update) with state already materialized so isEquals runs; ResourceLeakDetector reports 2 leaked buffers (expected: 0). Alternatively assert buf.refCnt()==0 after the call.

findings.bug: fastRemoveValueAsync accumulates the number of removed set members into the Lua variable 'size' via srem, but the script ends with 'return 0;', so the future always resolves to 0 regardless of how many values were actually removed.
findings.why_real: The method returns RFuture<Long> and the 'size' accumulator is computed then discarded (dead code); a fast* removal returning a count that is hardcoded to 0 contradicts both the accumulator's purpose and the Long return type. Correct code returns 'size'.
findings.how_to_prove: put(k, v1); put(k, v2); then long n = multimap.fastRemoveValue(v1, v2).get(); expected 2 (both members removed), actual 0.

findings.bug: The lastIndexOf loop uses condition `i > 0`, so index 0 is never examined and an element stored at index 0 is reported as not found (-1).
findings.why_real: The java.util.List#lastIndexOf contract requires returning the highest index i with Objects.equals(o, get(i)) or -1 if absent; the sibling indexOf on line 52 correctly iterates `i < len` covering index 0. The `i > 0` bound is an off-by-one that excludes index 0.
findings.how_to_prove: new ImmutableList<>(new String[]{"a"}).lastIndexOf("a") -> expected 0, actual -1. Also new ImmutableList<>(new String[]{"x","y"}).lastIndexOf("x") -> expected 0, actual -1.

findings.bug: equals is asymmetric and throws on a valid List argument: an ordinary List (e.g. ArrayList) compared TO an ImmutableList invokes AbstractList.equals which calls listIterator() on the ImmutableList, which throws UnsupportedOperationException.
findings.why_real: Object#equals requires symmetry: a.equals(b) == b.equals(a). AbstractList.equals(Object o) is implemented as `ListIterator e1 = listIterator(); ListIterator e2 = ((List)o).listIterator(); ...` — it calls listIterator() on the OTHER list. ImmutableList#listIterator() (line 197) throws UnsupportedOperationException, so the reverse comparison throws on valid input instead of returning true.
findings.how_to_prove: List<String> a = new ArrayList<>(java.util.Arrays.asList("a","b")); List<String> b = new ImmutableList<>(new String[]{"a","b"}); assertTrue(b.equals(a)) passes, but a.equals(b) throws UnsupportedOperationException instead of returning true (violates equals symmetry).

findings.bug: The Comparator returns -2 for CONFLICT for BOTH compare(a,b) and compare(b,a) when two types conflict (conflict is symmetric), so signum(compare(a,b)) == signum(compare(b,a)) == -1, violating the antisymmetry requirement.
findings.why_real: java.util.Comparator#compare contract requires signum(compare(x,y)) == -signum(compare(y,x)) for all x,y. compareTypes yields CONFLICT symmetrically (e.g. an object type vs a primitive type both map to CONFLICT via the symmetric branches at lines 100-105), and compare maps CONFLICT to -2 unconditionally, so both directions return a negative value rather than negatives of each other. This can trigger TimSort's 'Comparison method violates its general contract!' IllegalArgumentException when sorting collections containing conflicting types.
findings.how_to_prove: Take two conflicting ArgTypes t1 (an object) and t2 (a primitive int). comparator.compare(t1,t2) returns -2 and comparator.compare(t2,t1) also returns -2; assert Integer.signum(compare(t1,t2)) == -Integer.signum(compare(t2,t1)) fails (both -1).

findings.bug: The @param javadoc extraction regex has no word boundary after the parameter name, so a record component whose name is a prefix of another component's name matches the wrong @param line.
findings.why_real: The pattern String.format("(?<=@param +%s).*?...", paramName) uses a lookbehind of '@param +foo' which also matches the '@param foo' prefix inside '@param foobar'; getJavaDoc(RecordComponentElement) uses matcher.find() which returns the first match in document order, so component 'foo' can capture 'foobar's documentation. A word-boundary (\\b or a trailing separator) is required, as the sibling exact-name intent shows.
findings.how_to_prove: Build javadoc 'Some record.\n@param foobar the bar value\n@param foo real foo'; paramJavadocPattern("foo").matcher(doc).find() -> group() is 'bar the bar value' (from @param foobar) instead of the expected ' real foo'.

findings.bug: The self-reference guard 'resolved != typeVariable' only prevents a one-node cycle (A->A); a two-node mapping cycle (A->B, B->A) causes unbounded recursion and StackOverflowError.
findings.why_real: resolveGeneric recurses whenever the resolved value is a TypeVariable other than the key, but only compares against the immediate key, not the recursion chain; the class elsewhere (TypeExtractor.visitTypeVariable/hasCycle) explicitly guards against generic cycles, showing cycles are a real concern this method does not fully handle.
findings.how_to_prove: Populate a TypeDescriptor.generics map with two TypeVariables mapped to each other (A->B, B->A) and call resolveGeneric(A); expected a terminating result but actual is StackOverflowError.

findings.bug: getStartOfCurrentHour(zoneId) takes the current wall-clock time in UTC via LocalDateTime.now(UTC) and then reinterprets those same numeric fields as being in zoneId via atZone(zoneId), conflating UTC wall time with the target zone and producing an instant shifted by the zone offset.
findings.why_real: The correct semantics (as implemented by the sibling getStartOfCurrentMonth, which uses LocalDate.now(UTC)...atStartOfDay(zoneId), and by the standard idiom Instant.now().atZone(zoneId).truncatedTo(HOURS)) is to truncate the actual current instant in the target zone. LocalDateTime.now(UTC).atZone(zoneId) instead relabels UTC wall time as zoneId wall time. Verified numerically: at real instant 2026-07-01T14:30:00Z with zone America/New_York the method returns 2026-07-01T18:00:00Z instead of the correct 2026-07-01T14:00:00Z.
findings.how_to_prove: Freeze clock at 2026-07-01T14:30:00Z; call getStartOfCurrentHour(ZoneId.of("America/New_York")). Expected 1751378400000 (2026-07-01T14:00:00Z, the start of the hour containing 'now'); actual 1751392800000 (2026-07-01T18:00:00Z) — off by the -04:00 zone offset.

findings.bug: handlePubrec fetches pendingPublish = getPendingPublishes().get(messageId) and immediately dereferences it (pendingPublish.onPubackReceived()) without a null check, so an unexpected, duplicate, or already-completed PUBREC packet id causes a NullPointerException that propagates through the Netty pipeline.
findings.why_real: The sibling ACK handlers in the same class guard against exactly this: handleSubAck (line 219) and handleUnsuback (line 274) return early when the pending map lookup is null, and handlePuback (line 288) uses computeIfPresent. handlePubrec (and handlePubcomp at line 331) instead dereference the raw get() result, an inconsistency that turns a broker sending a PUBREC for an unknown/already-removed message id into an NPE.
findings.how_to_prove: Invoke channelRead0 with a PUBREC MqttMessage whose messageId is not present in client.getPendingPublishes(); expected: message ignored (as handleSubAck/handleUnsuback do for unknown ids); actual: NullPointerException at pendingPublish.onPubackReceived().

findings.bug: appendCharacters throws NullPointerException when called before any byte content has been flushed into 'result', because 'result' is still null.
findings.why_real: encodeCurrentBytesIfAny() only assigns 'result' when currentBytes.length() > 0; on a fresh builder currentBytes is empty so it stays null, then result.append(value) dereferences null. The method's Javadoc ('Appends the characters from value') states no precondition, so this is an NPE on valid usage.
findings.how_to_prove: new ECIStringBuilder().appendCharacters(new StringBuilder("x")) -> expected the characters appended (toString() == "x"), actual NullPointerException at 'result.append(value)'.
